name: Erik Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my brother-in-law, Pete Lund, at Lund Hill. Five hundred ewes, sixty beef cows and some spring barley. I'm out by seven, feeding the cattle in winter, checking sheep on the quad bike, mending walls and gates. Pete does the thinking and I do the carrying, and that suits me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to work there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I laid bricks for thirty years. At 55 my knees said enough, and Pete said come up the hill, there's always work for family. My wife Ruth is his sister. I'm three years in and I still can't lamb a ewe on my own if it's a bad one; Pete has to come.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside and being useful to family. I like Sunday chapel and a quiet pint after. What wears me out is the cold, and the knees, and the lamb price, because when it drops Pete gets short and I can see him worrying about my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you are, all that money spent on clever computers and the sheep still need a man on a quad bike. At chapel I'd say we should put our trust in work and family, not gadgets. I'm not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, and as they are is hard enough. Lamb price, feed price, Pete's overdraft. And Pete's boy Jack finishes agricultural college next year, so I wonder whether there'll still be room for an old bricklayer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on working at Lund Hill the same as ever. Ruth and I would cut back a bit, fewer trips to the coast, so we put more by. And I'd offer to take a smaller wage in a bad year, because that's what family does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not the computers, it's the money and my knees. It sits on me in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jack is coming home. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud of the lad, and a bit worried. Jack is young and quick and he knows all the new ways. When my nephew Jack comes home from college, Pete won't need an old bricklayer carrying feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Pete did let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete wouldn't, I don't think. But if he did, I'd look for work on the big estate down the valley, or go back to small building jobs if my knees let me. I wouldn't sit at home.

say: All that money on **clever computers**, and the sheep still need a man on a quad bike.
At chapel I'd say trust **work and family**, not gadgets.
think: Things stay as they are, and that's hard enough: **lamb price**, feed price, Pete's overdraft.
When Pete's son **Jack** finishes college, there may be no room for an old bricklayer.
do: Carry on working at **Lund Hill** the same as ever.
Cut **trips to the coast** so Ruth and I put more by.
Offer Pete a **smaller wage** in a bad year, because that's what family does.
feel: **Uneasy** in the evenings about money and my knees, not computers.
S0.quote: When my nephew Jack comes home from college, Pete won't need an old bricklayer carrying feed.
fieldNote: His job depends on **family loyalty** and a farm that runs on an overdraft.
The biggest threat he names is a **younger relative**, not AI.
He would accept **lower pay** rather than strain the family.

steps.text: Carry on feeding cattle and mending walls at Lund Hill
Skip the coast trips and put the money by

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say leave the clever stuff to the offices and let farmers farm. At chapel I'd say every generation has its new machine and we got through. I'd not say anything online, because I'm not on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's the paperwork side that changes, and that's Pete's and Jack's business. Jack will have an app for the sheep and the cattle passports. My work is carrying and mending, and robots for that are a long way off in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and see what Jack brings in before I worry. I'd not learn the apps; that's not for me. I'd just keep turning up at seven and doing a good day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, same as now. Not worse. Maybe a bit left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Jack asked you to use one of the apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jack to do that bit and give me the feed buckets. I'm 58, and I'd rather carry a hundred feed buckets than learn one more password.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should look after people whose office jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their families first, and their church, and then they should find new work, like I did when the building went. The government's not good at much except paperwork, and now the computers do that too.

say: Leave **the clever stuff** to the offices and let farmers farm.
Every generation has its **new machine**, and we got through.
think: The **paperwork** changes, and that's Pete's and Jack's business.
My **carrying and mending** work is a long way from robots in this world.
do: Carry on turning up at **seven** and doing a good day's work.
Wait and see what **Jack brings in** before worrying.
feel: **Uneasy**, same as now, and maybe a little **left behind**.
S1.quote: I'm 58, and I'd rather carry a hundred feed buckets than learn one more password.
fieldNote: He refuses **apps** outright and leaves them to the next generation.
He blames **government** more than technology and trusts family and church.
Steady Disruption hits the **farm office**, which he isn't part of.

steps.text: Keep turning up at seven to feed and mend at Lund Hill
Wait to see what Jack's new apps change before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big tech firms pushing it on us before anyone's ready, and they should be made to slow down. At chapel I'd say we look after each other. At the pub I'd say I'll believe a robot can catch a ewe on that hill when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm 63 and a robot can carry and mend and feed. Pete would keep me out of loyalty for a while, but if a robot costs less than me, the overdraft decides, not Pete. I'd have three years short of my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting every spare penny by now, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, and stop the coast trips altogether. I'd talk to Ruth about her doing more hours at the bakery. And I'd ask the chapel elders whether there's any work in the village for a man with a trowel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have some say over it, I'd hope, but I'd be frightened for the money. A robot on Lund Hill would cost my brother-in-law Pete less than my wages, and the overdraft doesn't do family loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Those three years before the robots come, what would they feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like waiting for a storm you can see over the hill. I'd work harder than ever, so Pete knows what he'd be losing. And I'd go to chapel and pray, which I do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family looks after each other. Would you ask your children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. Grace has three little ones and Daniel's in the army. I'd sooner do any job going than take money from my own children.

say: **Big tech firms** are pushing this before anyone's ready and should slow down.
I'll believe a robot can **catch a ewe** on that hill when I see it.
think: By **2031** I'm 63 and a robot can carry, mend and feed.
If a robot costs less than me, **the overdraft** decides, not Pete.
do: Put about **150 a month** by and stop coast trips altogether.
Ask Ruth about **more bakery hours** to steady our income.
Ask the **chapel elders** about village building work for a man with a trowel.
feel: **Anxious** and frightened for money, though I hope I'd still have some say.
S2.quote: A robot on Lund Hill would cost my brother-in-law Pete less than my wages, and the overdraft doesn't do family loyalty.
fieldNote: He separates **Pete's loyalty** from the farm's finances, which he fears will win.
He blames **big tech** and looks to chapel and family for support.
He'd take **any job** before taking money from his children.

steps.text: Put about 150 a month by and stop coast trips
Ask Ruth about more hours at the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better, but it's still the big firms setting the pace. At chapel I'd say pray and plan. At the pub I'd still not believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2034 means I'm 66 and on my pension by then. AGI in 2031 is Jack's business with the paperwork. So I'd probably get to the end of my working days at Lund Hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see, and keep saving a bit more each month, maybe seventy-five, as a cushion for the bad lamb years. I'd keep my head down at Lund Hill. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Same old worries about lamb prices and my knees, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change anything with Pete and Jack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives Jack time to sort his apps and Pete time to sort his overdraft. By the time any robot climbs Lund Hill, I'll be drawing my pension and watching from the chapel bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to do with that extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teach Jack how to build a dry stone wall properly. They don't teach that at college. Somebody should know it after I'm gone.

say: **Five years** is better, but the big firms still set the pace.
At chapel I'd say **pray and plan**.
think: Robots in **2034** come when I'm 66 and on my pension.
The 2031 AGI is **Jack's business** with the paperwork.
do: Wait and see, keeping my **head down** at Lund Hill.
Save about **seventy-five** extra each month as a cushion for bad lamb years.
feel: **Uneasy** about lamb prices and knees, but not frightened.
S3.quote: By the time any robot climbs Lund Hill, I'll be drawing my pension and watching from the chapel bench.
fieldNote: Five years' warning lets him reach **pension age** before robots arrive.
He'd pass on **dry stone walling** skills to Jack.
His **everyday worries** persist regardless of AI.

steps.text: Wait and see while keeping my head down at Lund Hill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people to sort themselves out. At chapel I'd say look after the young ones. I'd stay off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me. I'll be retired years before 2039. But the lamb price and Pete's overdraft don't wait for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Lund Hill till 66 and save what I can. I'd tell our grandson Sam to do a bricklaying apprenticeship rather than university. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the ordinary amount. Not about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bricklaying for Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's real work you can see at the end of the day. My grandson Sam should learn a trade with his hands, because a degree won't keep the rain off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete getting a rest. He's worked that hill since he was ten. If a robot carries the feed when he's 70, I'd not be sorry.

say: **Ten years** is plenty for people to sort themselves out.
At chapel I'd say **look after** the young ones.
think: It doesn't touch me, as I'll be **retired** years before 2039.
The **lamb price** and Pete's overdraft don't wait for robots.
do: Carry on at **Lund Hill** until 66 and save what I can.
Steer grandson Sam towards a **bricklaying apprenticeship** instead of university.
feel: **Uneasy** in the ordinary way, not about AI.
S4.quote: My grandson Sam should learn a trade with his hands, because a degree won't keep the rain off.
fieldNote: A decade's warning removes AI from his worries, but **farm money** stays.
He favours **apprenticeships** over degrees for his grandson.
He hopes robots might give **Pete** a rest in old age.

steps.text: Carry on at Lund Hill until 66
Steer grandson Sam towards a bricklaying apprenticeship

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It puts a robot on the hill when I'm 63 and Pete's overdraft would make the choice. What would help is fewer taxes and rules on small farms, so Pete can afford to keep family on. And apprenticeships for the young ones, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A man who has his family and his chapel can lose a job without losing himself. I've done it once already.

headlineQuote: A man who has his family and his chapel can lose a job without losing himself.
portrait: Erik is a **58-year-old** former bricklayer working for his brother-in-law Pete on a hill sheep and cattle farm.
He never uses AI, leaves apps to his nephew Jack, and relies on **family and chapel**.
His worries are **lamb prices**, Pete's overdraft and his knees, which keep him uneasy throughout.
He turns **anxious** in AGI by 2028, expecting the overdraft to beat loyalty when robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a robot would reach the hill when he's **63**.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer **taxes and rules** on small farms, and **apprenticeships** rather than handouts.
